lessons.plain: External storage keeps records after power is off. The DBMS reads pages into memory, and a file organization determines how records are placed for searches and updates.
goals: Explain pages, records, and I/O on external storage
Compare heap, sorted, and hashed file organizations
Choose a layout for equality lookups, ranges, and scans

topics.title: Data on external storage: pages and records
topics.definition: External storage is persistent storage such as an SSD or hard disk. A DBMS moves data between it and memory in page-sized units, so page layout affects query cost.
details: A page (or block) groups records and metadata. The DBMS usually reads or writes a whole page even when a query needs one small value.
A slotted page uses a slot directory to locate records. With variable-length records, record bytes can move inside the page while a slot number remains the reference.
Sequential scans read many pages in order; an index can reduce reads for selective lookups. If a query needs most rows, scanning the pages may be cheaper than following many index pointers.
topics.example: A search for one student among 1,000 pages may read many pages without an index. An index can point to the relevant page. A report that needs nearly every student may be faster as a full scan.

topics.title: Heap, sorted, and hashed files
topics.definition: A file organization decides where records are placed and how the DBMS searches for them.
details: Heap: place new records wherever space is available; insertion is simple, search may scan. Sorted: keep records ordered by a key; range queries are useful, insertion can be expensive.
Hash: compute a bucket from a key; equality search is fast, but the file is not ordered for ranges. Collisions may use overflow pages.
topics.example: Choose hashing for many equality lookups by student id; choose sorted data or a B+ tree for listing ids between two values.

topics.title: Buffers and RAID
topics.definition: A buffer pool keeps frequently used pages in memory. RAID spreads or mirrors data across disks for performance or availability.
details: The buffer manager pins pages in use, marks changed pages dirty, and later flushes them to disk. LRU and clock can choose an unpinned page to replace.
RAID can use striping to distribute blocks or mirroring to keep copies. RAID does not replace database backups.
topics.example: If several queries reuse a page already in the buffer, the DBMS may avoid another disk read.

worked.title: Choose a file layout for three jobs
worked.setup: A student table has many inserts, exact searches by sid, and reports for sid ranges.

steps.title: Frequent inserts
steps.body: Heap placement makes new records easy to add without maintaining sort order.

steps.title: Exact lookup by sid
steps.body: A hash organization can map sid to a bucket for equality queries. A separate index may still be needed for other access patterns.

steps.title: Range report
steps.body: Hash order does not help with sid between 100 and 200. Sorted storage or a B+ tree can find the first key and then scan neighbors.

worked.answer: There is no best file organization for every query. Choose based on the workload, and consider indexes when the table serves several patterns.

diagram.title: From a query to an external-storage page
diagram.caption: The buffer pool checks memory first and reads a database page from persistent storage on a miss.

lessons.exam: Explain external storage and pages, compare heap/sorted/hash file organizations, describe a slotted page, and choose a layout for a workload.

lessons.plain: An index is a smaller guide that points toward data pages. Its layout trades extra space and update work for faster searches.

topics.title: What an index does and when it helps
topics.definition: An index is an auxiliary structure that maps search-key values to record or page locations so a query can find selected rows without scanning every data page.
details: An index can speed selective equality and range queries, but it uses storage and must be updated when rows change.
A table scan can be faster when most rows are needed. The DBMS chooses between an index path and a scan based on the query and estimated cost.
topics.example: If a query requests one student id from a very large table, an index can jump near that row. If it requests every student, reading the table in order may cost less than visiting every index entry.

topics.title: Dense and sparse indexes
topics.definition: A dense index has an entry for every search-key value or record. A sparse index has fewer entries and searches within an ordered data page after locating the nearest index entry.
details: A sparse index needs the data file to be ordered on the search key. It often uses less space than a dense index.
An index entry stores a key and a pointer to a record or page.
topics.example: If a sparse index stores the first key of each page, searching for key 37 starts at the page whose first key is the greatest value not above 37.

topics.title: Primary, clustered, and secondary indexes
topics.definition: A primary index is on the ordering key of an ordered data file. A clustered index follows the physical order of a non-key field. A secondary index is on a field the data file is not ordered by.
details: Clustered access can retrieve nearby matching records with fewer page reads. A secondary/unclustered index may point to scattered pages.
Indexes use storage and must be maintained when records change, so they are not free.
topics.example: An enrollment file ordered by course id is clustered for course lookups; an index on student id may be secondary.

topics.title: Multilevel indexes and ISAM
topics.definition: A multilevel index places a small index over a larger index so each search narrows the page range.
details: ISAM is a static indexed sequential structure. The index levels stay fixed after creation, while new records may go to overflow pages.
Too many overflow pages slow searches; reorganizing can restore the main sequential layout.
topics.example: Search the top index, follow one pointer to a lower index, then reach the data page.

worked.title: Search using a sparse index
worked.setup: Data pages are ordered. The first keys in the pages are 10, 25, 40, and 55. Find key 37.

steps.title: Find the nearest index key below 37
steps.body: 25 is the greatest page-start key that is no larger than 37.

steps.title: Follow the page pointer
steps.body: The index points to the page that starts at 25. Key 37 must be on that page if it exists, or in its overflow area.

steps.title: Scan within the page
steps.body: Read the ordered records on that page until 37 is found or the next key is larger.

worked.answer: The sparse index narrows the search to one page range; ordering makes the final short scan possible.

diagram.title: An index narrows the search
diagram.caption: The entry points to a page; ordering finishes the lookup.

lessons.exam: Define dense and sparse indexes; compare clustered and secondary; explain multilevel indexing, ISAM, and the cost/benefit of an index.

lessons.plain: A B+ tree is a balanced index whose pages guide a search to a leaf. Its linked leaves make ordered and range searches efficient.
goals: Read a B+ tree node and separator
Trace a search and leaf split
Explain root growth, height, and range scans

topics.title: B+ tree structure
topics.definition: A B+ tree is a balanced, page-based search tree. Internal pages hold separator keys and child pointers; leaf pages hold data entries and are linked in key order.
details: All root-to-leaf paths have the same length. A high fanout lets each page point to many children, keeping the tree shallow.
In a common order-m convention, an internal node has at most m children and a non-root node has at least ceil(m/2); some texts define order by maximum keys instead, so state the convention.
topics.example: A search compares the target with separator keys at each internal page, follows one pointer, and checks the leaf.

topics.title: Search and insertion
topics.definition: Search follows separator ranges to a leaf. Insertion places a key in that leaf and splits a full page.
details: A leaf split keeps keys in order and copies a separator into the parent. If the parent is full, its split can continue upward.
If the root splits, a new root is created. The tree stays balanced because every leaf remains at the same depth.
topics.example: Insert 12, 18, and 25 into a full leaf. Divide the entries between two leaves and insert a separator for the right leaf in the parent.

topics.title: Range queries and B-tree comparison
topics.definition: After finding the first matching leaf, a range query follows leaf links through the sorted entries.
details: This makes B+ trees useful for equality searches and ranges. Bulk loading sorts entries into leaves first and then builds parent levels.
A B-tree may store data entries in internal nodes as well as leaves. A B+ tree keeps all data entries at leaves, which increases internal fanout and supports leaf scans.
topics.example: To list all students with sid from 100 to 160, find 100 once, then follow leaf links until the key exceeds 160.

worked.title: Insert into a full leaf
worked.setup: For a small teaching example, a leaf can hold at most two keys. The leaf currently has [12, 18]. Insert 25.

steps.title: Find the target leaf
steps.body: Compare 25 with the tree's separators and follow the pointer to the leaf [12,18].

steps.title: Insert in sorted order
steps.body: The temporary leaf is [12,18,25], which exceeds its two-key capacity.

steps.title: Split and promote a separator
steps.body: Split into [12,18] and [25]. Copy 25 into the parent as the separator for the new right leaf. If the parent is full, split it too.

worked.answer: The leaves remain sorted and at the same depth. A root split creates a new root, preserving balance.

lessons.exam: Draw a B+ tree and trace search, insert, split, root growth, and range scan. State the order convention and compare B+ trees with B-trees.

lessons.plain: Hashing calculates a bucket from a key. Dynamic hashing splits buckets as data grows; B+ trees are often better when the query needs a range.
goals: Trace extendible hashing depth and splits

topics.title: Static hashing
topics.definition: A hash function maps a search key to one of a fixed set of buckets.
details: Different keys can map to the same bucket; this is a collision. Overflow pages store records when the main bucket fills.
As a file grows, long overflow chains and skewed buckets can make search slower.
topics.example: With h(sid)=sid mod 4, ids 12 and 20 both map to bucket 0.

topics.title: Extendible hashing
topics.definition: Extendible hashing uses a directory of hash-bit prefixes and splits a bucket when it overflows.
details: Global depth is the number of hash bits used by the directory. Local depth says how many bits distinguish one bucket.
If a split needs more bits than the directory currently uses, double the directory. Only the overflowing bucket's records are redistributed.
topics.example: A bucket with local depth 1 splits using the next hash bit. If that raises local depth beyond global depth, double the directory.

topics.title: Linear hashing and range trade-off
topics.definition: Linear hashing grows gradually using a split pointer instead of doubling a directory all at once.
details: Both extendible and linear hashing adapt buckets as data grows, but they organize splits differently.
Hashing is designed for equality tests. Because bucket order is unrelated to key order, a range query usually cannot follow adjacent values. A B+ tree preserves that order.
topics.example: Find sid=140: a hash index can jump to its bucket. Find all ids from 100 through 160: a B+ tree can move through adjacent leaves.

worked.title: Split an extendible-hash bucket
worked.setup: Use the low bits of each key's hash. The directory has global depth 1 and one bucket has local depth 1. A new key causes that bucket to overflow.

steps.title: Inspect the bucket's local depth
steps.body: Local depth 1 means this bucket is currently distinguished by one hash bit.

steps.title: Split and redistribute
steps.body: Create a second bucket and use the next hash bit to separate the old and new records.

steps.title: Check the directory depth
steps.body: If local depth becomes greater than global depth, double the directory so it can address the new distinction. If not, only update the directory entries for the split bucket.

worked.answer: Only the overflowing bucket needs redistribution. Global depth controls directory size; local depth controls an individual bucket split.

lessons.exam: Compare static, extendible, and linear hashing. Trace overflow/split and compare hash-based with tree-based indexing for point and range queries.
